entries.name: Contrastive divergence
entries.definition: A parameter-learning algorithm for energy-based or product-of-experts models that replaces the equilibrium negative-phase expectation by configurations obtained from a short model-invariant Markov chain restarted at observed data, without differentiating through the chain distribution.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the customary contrastive-divergence update family, including CD-1 and CD-k, rather than only the formal difference-of-KL-divergences objective that motivated it. The number of transition steps is an algorithm parameter, not a separate architecture. It differs from persistent-chain learning, CD-PercLoss prediction search and pairwise representation-learning losses. The short aliases are contextual, not evidence of equivalence to every use of those initials. All 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 370 preceding native IDs/names/aliases were compared, with no normalized identity match. Fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files throughout both worktree and main, returning 29 lines each; all 22 unique matched contents were read. Hits described CD as a training component, a pending lead or a boundary from CD-PercLoss, not an existing candidate record. All 61 semantic label/synonym hits, 21 exact annotated AIO nodes with outgoing edges, corresponding generated records and four native neighbors were inspected. Previously fully read contextual files were verified byte-identical. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and inspected neighborhood.
limitations: A short-chain CD estimate is generally biased for the likelihood gradient and is not generally the exact negative gradient of the formal contrastive-divergence objective. A small objective or accurate reconstruction can coexist with poor global modeling when the chain mixes slowly.

The binary-RBM CD-1 field can have unequal cross partial derivatives, so it is not universally the gradient of any scalar objective. The inspected convergence paper also constructs cycling with a particular nonconvex regularizer; this is not a claim that ordinary L2-regularized CD always cycles. Existence of a regularized fixed point does not establish convergence to it.

Exact Gibbs transitions require sampled states. Conditional expectations can replace final sufficient statistics by Rao–Blackwellization, but feeding probability-valued states into later nonlinear transition conditionals defines a different approximation. Hinton Section 8 explicitly uses such a probability-valued visible reconstruction in its digit experiment; that variant is not silently equated to exact binary Gibbs CD.

The original simulations do not prove universal likelihood improvement, unbiased learning or global convergence. Their digit classification experiments also disclose test-set model selection; no reported ranking is adopted as a general property.

The algorithm is not tied to an RBM architecture, and the formal objective is not merely a difference of mean log likelihoods: distribution-entropy terms matter. No author implementation, training run or complete convergence theorem is certified.

claims.statement: For each observed example or minibatch, initialize a Markov chain at the data and perform k transitions with the model parameters held fixed. For an RBM, alternate sampled hidden and visible blocks, then compute hidden conditional expectations at the resulting visible configurations for the negative statistics. Update weights by a learning rate times observed-data minus k-step reconstructed visible-hidden statistics; update biases by the corresponding first-moment differences. More generally, contrast derivatives of the unnormalized log model at the data and chain endpoints, treating the endpoints as fixed for the update. The motivating objective is C_k(theta)=KL(q_data||p_theta)-KL(q_data T_theta^k||p_theta). Its exact derivative also contains the parameter dependence of the k-step distribution; the customary CD update omits that contribution. With a fixed ergodic kernel and sufficiently long chains, the negative expectation approaches the equilibrium expectation; a short-chain update does not assume that limit has been reached.

entries.name: Persistent contrastive divergence
entries.definition: A learning algorithm that estimates an energy model’s negative-phase statistics with Markov chains whose states persist across parameter updates, rather than restarting those chains at the current data minibatch.
entries.identity_notes: This is persistent contrastive divergence as presented for RBMs by Tieleman. Persistence refers to the fantasy-particle sampling state across learning updates, not continual-learning tasks or recurrent sequence-model state. It is an instance of persistent-chain stochastic-approximation learning, not the original data-restarted CD-k rule. Fast PCD adds temporary sampling parameters and remains a separate variant. All 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 370 preceding native IDs/names/aliases were compared, with no normalized identity match. Fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files throughout both worktree and main, returning 29 lines each; all 22 unique matched contents were read. Hits described CD as a training component, a pending lead or a boundary from CD-PercLoss, not an existing candidate record. All 61 semantic label/synonym hits, 21 exact annotated AIO nodes with outgoing edges, corresponding generated records and four native neighbors were inspected. Previously fully read contextual files were verified byte-identical. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and inspected neighborhood.
limitations: Finite transitions, correlated particles and changing parameters can leave negative statistics biased for the current equilibrium expectation. The small-learning-rate justification depends on mixing relative to parameter drift; it is not a guarantee at every finite step size.

A persistent chain is neither an independent model sample at each iteration nor a proof of rapid mixing. The original paper discusses difficulties when strong dependencies or large weights slow exploration, and the regularization and learning-rate schedule affect behavior.

Exact positive-phase inference is available for the binary RBM formulation inspected here; that property does not transfer automatically to models with interacting latent variables. The paper also examines fully visible MRFs with different update costs and sampling structure.

The fixed-R contrastive expression is an instantaneous derivative description. Particle evolution and parameter adaptation remain coupled; the ordinary data-restarted contrastive-divergence objective does not describe that entire process.

The retained particles and one-step experimental choice do not imply that conditional models with changing conditioning inputs have the same tracking problem as an unconditional RBM. No universal superiority, global convergence or author-code behavior is certified.

claims.statement: Maintain a collection of fantasy-particle configurations independently of which data minibatch is currently presented. Compute positive-phase sufficient statistics from that minibatch, using exact hidden conditional expectations for an RBM. Advance the existing fantasy particles by a small number of Gibbs transitions under the current model parameters and estimate negative-phase statistics from those particles. Update the model parameters from the positive-minus-negative difference and retain the particle states for subsequent iterations. The 2008 experiments use one full Gibbs step per update, one particle per minibatch member and no chain resets; those are specified experimental choices, while persistence is the defining distinction. If the chain distribution tracks the current equilibrium sufficiently closely, its negative statistics approximate those of the model. For fixed particle-distribution R, the instantaneous update can be expressed as the negative derivative of KL(q_data||p_theta)-KL(R||p_theta), with R held fixed; this does not make the whole coupled adaptive process descent on one fixed objective.

entries.definition: A persistent-chain RBM learning algorithm that adds rapidly updated, rapidly decaying auxiliary parameters to the sampling energy while retaining separate regular parameters for the model distribution.
entries.identity_notes: This is fast PCD from Tieleman and Hinton, not a generic fast implementation of PCD. Its temporary energy overlay is separate from the parameters defining the learned model. It differs from momentum alone, partial smoothing of positive gradients, ordinary persistent sampling and fast-weight memory architectures used for prediction. All 61 semantic label/synonym hits, 21 exact annotated AIO nodes with outgoing edges, corresponding generated records and four native neighbors were inspected. limitations: The negative phase uses a changing overlay and is not an unbiased equilibrium estimate for the base theta model merely because each conditional is tractable. Fast parameters intentionally change the sampling landscape; improved mixing is a motivation supported by particular experiments, not a universal guarantee.

Section 6 computes h-minus as a vector of conditional probabilities and then writes a visible draw conditioned on h-minus while calling this a full Gibbs update. Exact binary block Gibbs also requires drawing a hidden state; using the probability vector directly gives a distinct mean-field-style transition. This record preserves the intended combined-parameter sampling mechanism without certifying an uninspected implementation or silently resolving that pseudocode ambiguity.

The pseudocode computes negative statistics at the current particles before advancing them, then updates both parameter sets. Changing the ordering or using regular instead of combined parameters in the negative conditionals changes the stated procedure. Final conditional expectations for statistics and sampled states for transitions must be distinguished.

Fast decay, learning-rate schedules, particle count and initialization influence the procedure. The paper tests alternatives, and its 19/20 decay and 100 chains are not universal optimal settings. Fast PCD does not mean that fast parameters contribute to the final base model’s normalized density.

The source’s mixing discussion and restricted MNIST/Micro-NORB experiments do not certify global convergence, asymptotic unbiasedness, universally better likelihood or optimal general hyperparameters. No author-code or empirical-performance reproduction was performed.

claims.statement: Maintain regular parameters theta, auxiliary fast parameters phi and persistent visible configurations. Compute positive statistics using hidden conditional probabilities under theta given the data. Compute negative statistics at the fantasy configurations using hidden conditionals under theta+phi, and advance the persistent chains with the combined sampling parameters. Use the same positive-minus-negative statistic difference g to increment theta by eta_regular*g and set phi to rho*phi+eta_fast*g. The paper’s pseudocode uses rho=19/20, initializes fast parameters at zero and regular parameters at small random values, and uses 100 initially zero visible chains. Its initial experiments keep the fast learning rate constant while reducing the regular rate, and later examine alternative schedules. These numerical settings instantiate the method rather than defining every FPCD variant. The reported model probability is defined by theta alone; the fast overlay shapes fantasy-particle exploration and decays quickly.

limitations: Finite search does not certify the global conditional mode. Its approximate free-energy difference can be negative, and its update can be zero when the searched prediction equals the observed target even though another output has lower free energy.

Holding the prediction fixed is an explicit surrogate-update convention. It does not differentiate the sampling/selection process or produce the exact conditional log-likelihood gradient, and it does not guarantee calibrated conditional probabilities.

claims.statement: For training pair (u,v), initialize each visible value from the logistic input-to-visible prediction sigmoid(b_v+W_uv^T u) when those connections exist; without them, draw independent Bernoulli(0.5) visible values. Holding u fixed, perform k Gibbs updates and retain the k resulting visible configurations. Choose a configuration v_hat with the lowest conditional free energy among those candidates. Update model parameters using the derivative of F(v,u)-F(v_hat,u) with v_hat held constant, contrasting the observed and searched free-energy derivatives. This replaces the generally intractable global minimum in the generalized perceptron loss by a finite stochastic search. The source uses k mean-field updates instead of sampled Gibbs updates for test-time predictions. No partition function enters the frozen-prediction free-energy-difference gradient.
